tools.description: Point it at LinkedIn person profiles or company pages and it returns the posts a search engine has indexed for each one, as flat rows: permalink, author, a text excerpt, and the publish date decoded from the post id. No request is sent to LinkedIn and no cookie or account is used. A result counts only when its permalink names the source, so posts are never attributed to the wrong author. Coverage is what the search index holds: posts appear days or weeks after publishing and many never appear. Commenters, reaction counts, comment counts and media are no longer returned (removed 2026-10-12, they came only from LinkedIn pages). Rows carry row_type post or notice; filter on row_type before loading a table. post_id is the activity URN and is stable across runs. Every row carries degraded and degradation_reason. Requires an APIFY_TOKEN and consumes Apify credits. Read only.

tools.description: Give it a company domain and it returns the registered legal entity behind it: legal name, company number, jurisdiction, status, entity type, LEI and VAT number, as one flat row with a full audit trail of what was rejected and why. Three registers are queried: UK Companies House, GLEIF and SEC EDGAR. Register search endpoints are fuzzy and always return something, so by default a record is accepted only when the normalized legal names are identical. That is why roughly 6 domains in 10 resolve rather than 10 in 10, and why a null here is a trustworthy answer rather than a gap. Read match_method, match_confidence and rejected_candidates before acting on a match. Setting match_strictness to fuzzy will hand you a confidently wrong company on most domains and should be treated as a research mode, not a default.
